s-fc7-high-0.essay:
In Kazuo Ishiguro's The Remains of the Day, Stevens, the aging butler of Darlington Hall, talks constantly about dignity, polishing silver, and what makes a "great" butler. What he almost never talks about is what he has lost. Stevens's evasions, both in the conversations he remembers and in the way he narrates them, are meant to protect the professional dignity he has organized his whole life around. Ishiguro, however, uses the first-person narration to let the reader hear exactly what Stevens leaves out, so his silences end up working as a confession he never meant to make. In the end the novel suggests that the dignity Stevens worships is really a habit of not looking, and that this habit cost him love and also made him complicit in his employer's politics.

The clearest example is the death of Stevens's father during the international conference of 1923. While his father is dying upstairs, Stevens keeps serving the guests downstairs. When Miss Kenton tells him his father has died, he does not go up, and he lets her see to the body. Telling it years later, Stevens spends more time on a guest's sore feet and the success of the evening than on his own grief, and he says he remembers that night with a sense of triumph. The reader notices the gap right away. A man who really felt triumphant would not need to keep coming back to the night and defending it. Stevens's restraint keeps him composed in front of the most powerful men in Europe, and it also stops him from being a son at the one moment that called for it. Here silence protects him and costs him in the same act.

His silences with Miss Kenton follow the same pattern but are harder to read, because romance is the thing Stevens most refuses to name. When she catches him reading a sentimental love story in his pantry, he will not let her see it, and later he explains he was only reading to improve his vocabulary. That excuse is itself an evasion, and Ishiguro makes it a little funny so we can see how hard Stevens is working to avoid the obvious. The most painful moment comes after Miss Kenton tells him she has accepted a proposal. Stevens finds her crying behind her parlour door, stands in the corridor, and does not knock. He moves straight on to business about the important visitors upstairs. He describes the closed door carefully but never his own feelings, so the door stands in for everything he cannot say. Years later, when he visits her as Mrs. Benn and she admits she sometimes imagines the life she could have had with him, he finally admits, briefly, that his heart was breaking. The delay of decades is the point: by the time he can say it, saying it changes nothing.

Ishiguro does not keep these silences private, though. Stevens is just as evasive about Lord Darlington. When Darlington orders him to dismiss two Jewish maids in the 1930s, Stevens obeys without protest and later tells Miss Kenton he had been upset all along, which she resents because he never said so at the time. On his trip he even denies having worked for Darlington to avoid awkward questions. These lies of omission link Stevens's personal habit to a national one: the English upper class that preferred good manners and loyalty to facing what appeasement actually meant. Stevens's idea of dignity, never showing what you think, turns out to be exactly what let people like Darlington go unquestioned.

Some readers see Stevens as simply loyal, a man of real integrity in a job that asked for self-control. The novel does respect his skill. But the ending at the pier in Weymouth, where he cries in front of a stranger and wonders what dignity there is in having trusted Darlington, shows that his silence has not protected his dignity so much as emptied it. Stevens is the last person to understand why he kept quiet, and Ishiguro's real achievement is making the reader understand it first.

s-fc7-high-1.essay:
In Kazuo Ishiguro's The Remains of the Day, Stevens, the aging butler of Darlington Hall, narrates his whole life without saying the two things that matter most: that he loved Miss Kenton, and that the master he served so faithfully was badly wrong. His silence is not just a personality quirk. Ishiguro shows that the "dignity" Stevens prizes is built out of refusals to speak, and that the same restraint that protects Stevens from pain is what empties his life out. Because Stevens narrates the novel himself, the reader hears his silences long before he does, and the book becomes less a story about a butler than a story about how a person can lose his own life by declining to name it.

The clearest early example is the night his father dies during the 1923 conference at Darlington Hall. Stevens keeps serving the guests while his father is dying upstairs, and when Miss Kenton tells him his father has passed, he does not go up right away. Later, telling the story, he says he looks back on that night with a sense of triumph. What he leaves out is any grief at all. The gap between the word "triumph" and what actually happened is where Ishiguro wants us to look. Stevens frames his silence as professionalism, but the reader sees a son who cannot admit what his job has cost him. This scene sets up the pattern for the rest of the novel: the more important the feeling, the more carefully Stevens talks around it.

His relationship with Miss Kenton follows the same pattern, but here the silence hurts someone else too. When she catches him reading a sentimental romance novel, he insists he reads such books only to improve his command of English. The excuse is almost funny, but it is a small version of his whole problem, since he would rather be thought odd than be caught feeling something. Later, after Miss Kenton tells him she has accepted Mr. Benn's proposal, Stevens stands outside her door, believes she is crying, and says nothing. He goes back downstairs to the business of the house. Ishiguro puts the moment in Stevens's own voice, so the restraint is the narration itself, and we feel the door between them as a literal and emotional barrier. His silence does show a kind of loyalty, to the house and to his idea of a great butler, but it is loyalty to an abstraction at the expense of an actual person.

Some readers might argue that Stevens is simply a product of his class and era, and that his silence is less a personal failure than a role English service demanded. That reading is fair, and Ishiguro clearly connects Stevens's restraint to a fading English ideal. But the novel does not let him off the hook completely. His silence about Lord Darlington, who hosted pro-German meetings and had two Jewish maids dismissed, shows that the same habit has political consequences. Stevens carried out the dismissals, and on his trip he even denies having worked for Darlington when strangers ask. Here silence stops protecting his dignity and starts protecting his complicity. The evasion that kept him from grieving his father now keeps him from facing his part in something shameful, which suggests that personal and moral blindness come from the same source.

By the end, the silence cracks only a little. After meeting Mrs. Benn in the West Country, where she admits she sometimes imagines the life she might have had with him, Stevens finally weeps on a pier to a stranger and concedes he gave his best to Lord Darlington. Yet even then he decides to practice bantering for Mr. Farraday. The reader understands that he has glimpsed the truth and is already folding it back into duty. Ishiguro's point is unsettling: silence can feel like strength, but held long enough, it becomes the whole shape of a life, and recognition arrives only when there is little left to change.

s-fc7-mid-0.essay:
In Kazuo Ishiguro's The Remains of the Day, Stevens the butler almost never says what he feels, and this silence shows the reader what he cannot admit to anyone, including himself: that he loved Miss Kenton and that he wasted his life serving a man who did not deserve it. Stevens's restraint is supposed to be dignity, but the novel shows that it is really a way of hiding from his own regret, and that it costs him the only real relationship he could have had.

The clearest example is how Stevens deals with Miss Kenton. When she tries to get closer to him, he answers with talk about work. In the scene where she finds him reading a sentimental novel in his pantry, he is embarrassed and tells her it is only to improve his language. Ishiguro lets the reader see that he is hiding something, because Stevens as narrator explains it away as if nothing happened. Later, when Miss Kenton tells him she has been offered a marriage proposal, Stevens only says that he wishes her well and goes back to his duties. The reader can tell that this is the moment he could have spoken, and the fact that he says nothing makes the loss bigger. Even years later, when they meet again, he does not say what he feels. He only says that he is glad of her letter and talks about the staff shortage at Darlington Hall. His silence protects him from being hurt, but it also hurts Miss Kenton, who clearly wanted him to say something.

Stevens also stays silent about Lord Darlington. He does not argue when Darlington decides to dismiss the two Jewish maids, even though he privately thinks it is wrong, and later he even denies having worked for Darlington when strangers ask. These moments show that Stevens's loyalty is a kind of evasion. He tells himself that a good butler does not judge his employer, but his silence means he helped do something wrong. The first person narration makes this stronger, because Stevens is telling the story himself and keeps leaving things out or changing the subject. The reader slowly understands more than he does, which is the irony of the book.

By the end, when Stevens sits on the pier at Weymouth and finally admits that his heart was breaking, it is a small crack in his silence. He still turns to the idea of "bantering" as a way to move forward, which suggests he has not completely changed. This shows that his silence is both protection and punishment. It kept him safe from embarrassment, but it left him with only the remains of his day. Ishiguro uses Stevens's withheld speech to criticize a whole idea of English dignity that makes people confuse emptiness with duty.

s-fc7-mid-1.essay:
In The Remains of the Day, Stevens almost never says what he feels, and the things he leaves out show what he cannot admit to himself. His silence is meant to look like dignity, but it actually hides his love for Miss Kenton and his regret about serving Lord Darlington. Ishiguro uses Stevens as a narrator who avoids the truth so that the reader sees it before he does, and this makes the novel a tragedy about a life wasted on professional restraint.

The clearest example is Stevens's relationship with Miss Kenton. When she tries to get closer to him, he answers with talk about work, like staff plans or the details of running the house. She also catches him reading a sentimental novel, and he becomes defensive and explains it away as a way to improve his language. This shows that he is embarrassed by feeling and covers it with a duty excuse. The most painful moment is when Miss Kenton tells him she has accepted a marriage proposal. Stevens says almost nothing and congratulates her, then goes back to his duties. Later he even notices that he has been crying, but he only mentions it briefly. His silence protects him from being vulnerable, but it also costs him the one person who might have made him happy.

Stevens's silence also covers his moral failure. He does not speak up against Lord Darlington's sympathy for the Germans, even when two Jewish maids are dismissed. He tells himself it is not his place to have opinions, and he repeats the idea of "dignity" as a reason. When people on his trip ask if he worked for Lord Darlington, he denies it. This is a lie of omission that shows his shame. His silence here punishes other people, like the maids, while it protects his own idea of himself.

His father's death is another example. Stevens keeps working during an important conference while his father is dying upstairs, and he describes it as a proud moment. The narration is calm, which makes the reader feel how much he is holding back. The first-person narration is important in the whole book, because Stevens tells the story himself and so his gaps and changes of subject become clues. The reader slowly learns more than he says.

At the end, on the pier at Weymouth, Stevens finally admits to a stranger that his heart is breaking, but then he turns to the idea of improving his banter. So even the confession is brief and he goes back to his old habits. This suggests that silence has become so much a part of him that he cannot completely escape it. Overall, Ishiguro shows that withheld speech can protect a person, but it can also hide the truth from the person himself until it is too late.
